=== FINDINGS FROM google_gemini-3_1-flash-lite ===
- scripts/security_audit.sh:2064-2071 | severity=MAJOR | confidence=4
  PROBLEM: The module_stem function now returns module stems regardless of length (e.g., 1-character stems).
  WHY: When a short module name (e.g., 'a.py' -> 'a') is deleted, the `deletion_block_reason` logic incorrectly treats any other file containing that word as having a guard reference that was removed. Because 'a' is a common article, this leads to many false-positive security findings that are incorrectly marked as blocking, causing unnecessarily strict security pass failures for pre-existing findings.
=== END FINDINGS FROM google_gemini-3_1-flash-lite ===

=== FINDINGS FROM minimax_minimax-m3 ===
- scripts/security_audit.sh:2064-2071 | severity=MAJOR | confidence=4
  PROBLEM: Removing the 3-character minimum length check allows single-character module stems (e.g. "a" from "a.py", "i" from "i.py") to match ordinary English text in cited files.
  WHY: With the current word-boundary regex `(?<![A-Za-z0-9_]){stem}(?![A-Za-z0-9_])`, a standalone "a" in any prose, comment or even Python identifier like "for a in items" matches the module stem "a". When a project deletes a single-character file (a.py, i.py), any pre-project finding whose cited file contains the standalone letter "a" gets incorrectly classified as blocking under `cited_file_references_module_with_deletions`. The security pass then files a fix issue and consumes a fix cycle for a non-existent guard. The justification comment says "a short module such as db.py or io.py can hold the deleted guard" — those are 2-char examples, but the implementation also accepts 1-char stems, which collide with common English text. A targeted mitigation would preserve the new 2-char case while still rejecting 1-char (e.g. `return stem if len(stem) >= 2 else ""`).
=== END FINDINGS FROM minimax_minimax-m3 ===

=== FINDINGS FROM openai_gpt-6-luna ===
- scripts/security_audit.sh:2069-2071, 2146-2149 | severity=MAJOR | confidence=5
  PROBLEM: `module_stem()` now accepts one-character stems, which the cited-file check matches as standalone words.
  WHY: If a project deletes an unrelated module such as `a.py`, a pre-existing finding’s cited file containing the lowercase word “a” matches this regex. `deletion_block_reason()` then marks the finding blocking, and the classifier counts it as blocking instead of advisory (lines 2211-2213, 2226-2229). This turns an unrelated deletion into a false security-pass blocker.
=== END FINDINGS FROM openai_gpt-6-luna ===
